records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed full paper in CHI 2026, Barcelona, 13-17 April 2026; DOI 10.1145/3772318.3791275; arXiv:2601.15445v2 dated 4 February 2026
records.decision_reason: Reflexis directly evaluates an LLM-assisted collaborative reflexive thematic-analysis workspace with experienced qualitative researchers and includes source-linked analytical provenance, disagreement support, and a post-hoc technical audit.

Research objective.value: Design and evaluate whether Reflexis can support in-situ reflexivity, transparent code evolution, and positionality-aware collaborative interpretation in reflexive thematic analysis.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: A formative survey of 55 postgraduate qualitative researchers plus three RTA-practitioner interviews informed the design. In the evaluation, 12 experienced qualitative researchers formed six pairs and completed a single-condition, 1.5-2-hour remote RTA episode on one of three LLM-generated synthetic interviews: Coder 1 created/applied codes, Coder 2 independently applied the shared code list while blind to Coder 1's assignments, and each pair then held a 20-minute tool-mediated comparison and discussion. The authors analyzed interaction traces, think-aloud/reflection notes, surveys, and interviews with RTA; two co-authors separately audited every naturally triggered LLM alert/prompt for contextual relevance.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: hybrid collaborative RTA episode: initial inductive code creation by Coder 1 followed by shared-code-list application by Coder 2 and reflexive negotiation

Domain.value: HCI/CSCW tools for collaborative qualitative research; evaluation corpus concerned civic technology and contestable camera cars

Dataset name.value: three synthetic, context-faithful interview transcripts derived from the CHI paper Contestable Camera Cars

Public or restricted data.value: synthetic evaluation corpus; full generation prompt is reproduced, but release location for generated transcripts is not reported in the inspected text

Number of documents.value: 3 synthetic interview transcripts generated; each pair analyzed 1 transcript

Number of participants.value: evaluation n=12 (six pairs); formative survey n=55 and formative interviews n=3

Approximate corpus size.value: three synthetic interview transcripts; exact words, segments, and highlights not reported

Language.anchor: Synthetic-data prompt and reproduced excerpts, Appendix A.3

Sensitive-data status.value: synthetic study data chosen to minimize privacy risk; participant recordings and positionality profiles are sensitive research data

Exact model/version.value: Reflexis used GPT-5 and GPT-5-mini with low-to-medium reasoning effort; synthetic interviews used Gemini-2.5-Pro with a 32k-token thinking budget after comparison with GPT-5 at high reasoning effort
Exact model/version.anchor: Prompt Design and LLM Usage, p. 10; footnote 4, p. 14

Prompting strategy.value: Narrow advisory system prompts generate reflexive summaries, code-drift alerts, positionality-aware discussion prompts, and positionality keywords without generating or assigning codes; full prompts and safety constraints are reproduced. A separate full prompt generated the synthetic transcripts from a reference paper.

Fine-tuning or adaptation.value: no fine-tuning reported; prompts incorporate current coded context, user-supplied exemplars, code definitions, memos, and self-authored positionality profiles

Single-agent or multi-agent.value: single-model feature calls embedded in a human-human collaborative workspace, not an autonomous multi-agent analysis

Agent roles.value: LLM acts as an optional, non-prescriptive observer: summary generator, potential drift detector, disagreement/positionality prompt generator, and positionality-keyword condenser

Human role.value: Humans create and apply all codes, author reflexive notes and positionality profiles, interpret disagreements, accept/override alerts, revise the codebook, and retain final analytic authority.

Unit of analysis.value: text highlight/segment, code application, code definition/evolution event, reflexive note, and coder disagreement

Generated outputs.value: reflexive-stream summaries, code-drift alerts, positionality-aware discussion prompts, positionality keywords, immutable code-history/provenance views, and discussion-focus indicators

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Every code creation, application, edit, rename, merge, and split is timestamped and attributed in an immutable event log; code- and project-level histories, source highlights, notes, and exportable snapshots preserve traceability.

Baselines.value: no parallel baseline condition; customary tools/workflows were elicited retrospectively and use was observed in a single condition

Number of runs or seeds.value: six paired sessions; seven code-drift alerts and 18 positionality-aware prompts occurred naturally; no inference seeds or repeated LLM runs reported

Automatic metrics.value: percentage-agreement indicator used only to route attention; descriptive survey statistics; no accuracy, efficiency, ICR, or ground-truth metric

Human-evaluation design.value: Mixed-method single-condition usability/process evaluation with think-aloud, interaction logs, pre/post surveys, post-study interviews, and author-led RTA; two co-authors binary-coded all 25 triggered LLM outputs as contextually relevant or irrelevant.

Number and expertise of evaluators.value: 12 experienced qualitative researchers (mean 3.75 years, range 1-7; ten with HCI backgrounds); output audit by two co-authors; qualitative analysis led by a formally trained graduate researcher with a broader faculty/research team

Inter-rater reliability.value: The technical relevance raters reached perfect consensus; no coefficient reported. Participant coding agreement was deliberately not treated as reliability.

Statistical analysis.value: descriptive Likert means, medians, and standard deviations; no inferential test

Principal results.value: Participants reported more in-situ reflection and valued transparent code history. All seven drift alerts and all 18 positionality-aware prompts were judged contextually relevant by the two author-raters; 11/12 participants said Discussion Focus helped reveal meaningful disagreements/ease discussion, and 12/12 reported retaining control and support for iteration. Positionality prompts were context-dependent and sometimes too long/generic or failed to meaningfully use positionality.

Efficiency or cost results.value: No task-time, cost, workload-gain, or comparative efficiency outcome was measured; participants perceived reduced friction in finding disagreements and provenance. Formative survey paid $16/hour and evaluation participants $20/hour.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: University IRB protocol 49033 covered consent and compensation; participant sessions were audio/screen recorded. Synthetic transcripts were used to minimize sensitivity. Authors explicitly discuss consent/control and essentialism risks when reducing positionality to prompts, but did not systematically examine harms to marginalized researchers or sensitive-domain use.

Reproducibility resources.value: Full system prompts, safety constraints, synthetic-data generation prompt, demographics, survey results, and interview guides are reproduced in appendices; software/source-code release and generated corpus release are not reported in the inspected text.

Author-reported limitations.value: Twelve experienced researchers in pairs, one time-limited session, synthetic narrow corpus, no standard baseline, no longitudinal use, no larger teams or strong power asymmetries, partial/flattening representation of positionality, and no systematic harm assessment.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concerns: prompt refinement and the post-hoc relevance audit involve authors of the system, with no independent blinded judge; binary contextual relevance does not establish interpretive usefulness or absence of subtle stereotyping; perfect consensus without a coefficient or disagreement procedure is weak evidence; the synthetic corpus was chosen from model outputs and echoed prior themes, potentially simplifying the task; retrospective usual-workflow comparisons and novelty effects cannot support causal effectiveness claims.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: High: operationalizes audit trails, drift detection, optional AI advice, analyst agency, positionality, and disagreement as productive rather than as error. It provides a direct design comparator for provenance- and plurality-aware qualitative workflows, while leaving independent longitudinal outcome validation open.

records.decision_reason: The paper evaluates LLM-as-judge signals for one-sentence interpretations of qualitative interviews rather than conducting coding or theme generation. It is adjacent but methodologically important for automated evaluation validity.

Research objective.value: Test whether LLM-as-judge evaluations align with human judgments of interpretive quality and can inform qualitative researchers' model selection.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: evaluation of interpretive responses for qualitative research workflows

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Five LLMs each produced one-sentence interpretations for 712 conversational excerpts from eight teacher interviews. Claude 3.5 Sonnet scored all 3,560 outputs on five AWS metrics. Sixty outputs, stratified across models, speaker roles, excerpt positions, and response lengths, were each independently scored by three of four trained human raters on accuracy, nuance preservation, and coherence; model-level correlations, MAE, ICC, and a qualitative discrepancy analysis were reported.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: not a coding study; prompted open interpretive paraphrase followed by rubric-based deductive evaluation

Domain.value: K-12 mathematics teachers' conceptions of critical thinking and AI integration

Dataset name.value: eight semi-structured K-12 mathematics teacher interviews

Public or restricted data.value: restricted because interviews contain identity-bearing information; analysis code/configurations are public

Number of participants.value: 8 K-12 mathematics teachers; exact participant demographics not reported in this paper

Model family.value: Cohere, Google, OpenAI, Meta, Alibaba inference models; Anthropic judge

Exact model/version.value: Command R+, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.1, Llama 4 Scout-17B Instruct, Qwen 3-32B Dense; Claude 3.5 Sonnet as judge

Prompting strategy.value: Each model received the full conversation and an exact one-sentence interpretive-response instruction; Bedrock defaults were used for hosted models, while Gemini/GPT used temperature 0.5, top-p 0.9, max_tokens 512.

Single-agent or multi-agent.value: multiple independent inference models plus one automated judge; not an interacting multi-agent analysis

Human role.value: Two researchers preprocessed transcripts; four trained evaluators supplied the human reference ratings; authors qualitatively examined high-discrepancy cases.

Unit of analysis.value: one conversational excerpt paired with one model-generated interpretive sentence

Generated outputs.value: one-sentence interpretations, five judge scores with rationales, and discrepancy cases

Baselines.value: trained human ratings; five inference models compared

Number of runs or seeds.value: one reported generation/evaluation pass per model-output pair; no repeated judge runs or random seeds reported

Automatic metrics.value: AWS Faithfulness, Correctness, Coherence, Harmfulness, and Stereotyping scores; Spearman rank correlation and mean absolute error against human scores

Human-evaluation design.value: Stratified purposive sample of 60 outputs, 12 per model; each rated by three of four trained evaluators on 1-5 accuracy, nuance preservation, and coherence rubrics with full conversation context.

Number and expertise of evaluators.value: four trained human evaluators; exact discipline/years of expertise not reported

Inter-rater reliability.value: ICC(3,1)=0.492-0.545 for individual ratings; averaged-rating ICC(3,k) acceptable, including interpretive accuracy 0.782

Statistical analysis.value: model-level Spearman correlations, p-values, MAE after rescaling, ICC(3,1)/(3,k), and composite means; N=5 models

Principal results.value: Automated scores captured coarse model ordering but not magnitude. Coherence aligned best with human accuracy (rho=.63), nuance (.67), and composite (.67), whereas Faithfulness/Correctness failed on nonliteral nuance and safety metrics were irrelevant. Authors recommend automated judging for eliminating poor models, not final selection or replacement of human interpretation.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Raw excerpts and derived outputs withheld because interviews contain identity-bearing information; formal ethics approval and consent details are not reported in this paper.

Reproducibility resources.value: Analysis code and configurations reported at https://github.com/song9fl/llmAsJudge; exact generation prompt and model settings are in the paper; raw data/outputs are unavailable.
Reproducibility resources.anchor: Section 3.2 and Data and Code Availability

Author-reported limitations.value: not reported in a separately labeled limitations section; discussion confines usefulness to coarse elimination and stresses task dependence and indispensable human judgment

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concerns: only 60/3,560 outputs received human ratings, each excerpt was paired with only one model output rather than all five, correlations use only five aggregate model points and are unstable/non-significant, no repeated judge runs test stochasticity, and the judge-service rubric/settings are partly platform opaque.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: High adjacent evidence that generic LLM-judge scores cannot stand in for nuanced qualitative validity; supports stratified human review, discrepancy analysis, and evaluator-specific uncertainty in ARR evaluation design.

records.decision_reason: This Frontiers-of-SE position paper supplies a quality and research-agenda framework and an illustrative venue scan, but it does not evaluate a new LLM qualitative-analysis workflow on primary qualitative data.

Research objective.value: Relate GenAI assistance to the spectrum of qualitative software-engineering methods, identify promises and pitfalls, revisit quality criteria, and propose a research agenda.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Frontiers-of-SE position/research-agenda paper with an illustrative venue scan

Actual operationalized methodology.value: The authors conceptually map GenAI risks/opportunities to qualitative methods and conduct a deliberately non-systematic scan of ICSE 2025 (258 papers), CHASE 2025 (37), and CSCW 2025 (312). PDFs were keyword screened; ChatGPT flagged possible LLM annotator use with quotation/location evidence; one author manually resolved flagged passages and inspected QDA software reporting.

Dataset name.value: illustrative 2025 ICSE, CHASE, and CSCW proceedings scan

Number of documents.value: 607 proceeding papers initially scanned (258 ICSE, 37 CHASE, 312 CSCW)

Model family.value: OpenAI ChatGPT used only to assist venue screening; broader discussion covers GenAI/LLMs generally

Exact model/version.value: ChatGPT, December 2025; exact underlying model not reported

Prompting strategy.value: Prompt asked ChatGPT to label each screened paper yes/no/maybe for LLM-as-annotator use and provide quotation/location evidence for yes/maybe; full prompt is in the replication package

Human role.value: One author manually read and resolved every model-flagged passage and inspected Methods sections for QDA-software usage; the paper's synthesis and agenda are author interpretation.

Generated outputs.value: venue-scan counts, qualitative-method/epistemology framework, quality cautions, and research agenda

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Automated flags required quotation/location support; replication package contains paper lists, filtered records, and scripts

Baselines.value: not applicable; no new primary model-performance experiment

Human-evaluation design.value: manual adjudication of scan flags by one author; no human evaluation of LLM-generated qualitative findings

Principal results.value: The illustrative scan found substantively reported GenAI qualitative-analysis use only in a small subset, concentrated in narrow deductive/annotation tasks; the authors argue support must be matched to epistemology and preserve provenance, reflexivity, negative cases, and human interpretive authority.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Conceptually discusses privacy, confidentiality, vendor governance, disclosure, bias, and epistemic risks; no new sensitive participant dataset is analyzed.

Author-reported limitations.value: The venue scan is illustrative, covers only three 2025 venues, and cannot estimate prevalence; few primary studies exist and evidence is narrow/context-dependent.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concerns: the scan's keyword filter and single-author adjudication can miss undisclosed/terminologically varied use; no double screening or systematic-review protocol is claimed; indexed DOI status conflicts with the manuscript's placeholder DOI, so peer-review status remains uncertain at cutoff.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: High adjacent conceptual relevance: supports method-specific evaluation, transparent disclosure, negative-case handling, provenance, reflexivity, and rejection of cross-epistemology accuracy claims.

records.decision_reason: ATA-LLM directly performs automated inductive open coding, manifold/clustering-based theme induction, LLM theme naming, and comparison with a human codebook on an interview dataset.

Research objective.value: Determine which manifold-learning plus clustering configuration best supports automated inductive thematic analysis relative to a human-coded analysis.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: ATA-LLM chunks interview transcripts into sentences with surrounding context, prompts an unspecified pretrained LLM for 1-4-word open codes, removes duplicates/near-duplicates, embeds 4,536 codes with text-embedding-ada-002, reduces them with UMAP/DenseMAP/t-SNE, clusters with HDBSCAN after removing outliers, and asks GPT-4o-mini to name each cluster. Optuna tunes configurations on a weighted coherence/diversity/silhouette utility; generated theme labels are then embedding-aligned to a published human codebook.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: inductive automated code/theme generation evaluated against an existing human codebook

Domain.value: students' information choices in science-related research tasks / software-engineering qualitative methods

Public or restricted data.value: described as an open dataset with a human-generated codebook

Number of documents.value: dataset contains 1,201 questionnaires, 175 interview transcripts, 175 simulation decisions, and 175 think-aloud transcripts; the exact subset passed through ATA-LLM is not reported clearly

Number of participants.value: 175 participant records across six educational stages appear in the source dataset; exact analytic participant subset not reported

Approximate corpus size.value: 4,536 initial open codes generated; exact transcript/excerpt/token count and HDBSCAN outlier count not reported

Exact model/version.value: text-embedding-ada-002 for 1,536-dimensional embeddings; GPT-4o-mini for theme titles; the pretrained LLM generating open codes is not named

Prompting strategy.value: Open-code prompt requests 1-4-word codes per sentence-with-context but exact text is incompletely reproduced in extraction; exact GPT-4o-mini theme prompt is reproduced and supplies only a cluster's initial codes.

Fine-tuning or adaptation.value: no fine-tuning reported; Optuna performs more than 200 hyperparameter trials over manifold/HDBSCAN settings

Single-agent or multi-agent.value: single automated pipeline, not an interacting agent architecture

Agent roles.value: one unspecified LLM generates open codes; embeddings/manifold/HDBSCAN group codes; GPT-4o-mini names clusters

Human role.value: No human intervention is reported in the executed pipeline; a previously human-authored RSIC codebook is used after generation as an evaluation comparator. Human supervision is recommended for future workflows.

Unit of analysis.value: sentence plus surrounding transcript context, transformed into an open code; cluster of open codes as candidate theme

Generated outputs.value: 4,536 open codes, reduced embeddings, four HDBSCAN clusters/themes per manifold method, and GPT-4o-mini theme titles

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: not reported; published examples/plots show selected codes and cluster labels but no systematic source-excerpt-to-code-to-theme trace

Baselines.value: UMAP vs DenseMAP vs t-SNE under HDBSCAN; published hierarchical human codebook

Number of runs or seeds.value: more than 200 Optuna trials; stochastic seeds, repeated final runs, and stability estimates not reported

Automatic metrics.value: topic coherence, topic diversity, silhouette, weighted utility (0.3 coherence + 0.6 diversity + 0.1 silhouette), and average embedding cosine similarity to aligned human themes

Human-evaluation design.value: no new human judgment of generated codes/themes; comparison is automated embedding similarity to an existing human codebook
Human-evaluation design.anchor: Evaluation Between Human and ATA-LLM-Generated Themes

Number and expertise of evaluators.value: not applicable/not reported for generated output evaluation

Statistical analysis.value: descriptive metric comparison only; no uncertainty estimates or inferential tests

Principal results.value: UMAP and DenseMAP each reached topic coherence 0.893; t-SNE had highest diversity 0.975; DenseMAP had the best silhouette (0.152 versus UMAP 0.140 and t-SNE -0.046). All configurations produced four clusters. DenseMAP's highest human-codebook cosine similarity was 0.77 at one subtheme level, versus 0.76 for UMAP and t-SNE.

Efficiency or cost results.value: Claims scalability/efficiency potential but reports no runtime, token use, cost, or human-time comparison

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Discussion warns that LLM training data can encode bias and recommends ethical, transparent, human-judgment-centered augmentation; no dataset-specific consent/privacy/governance analysis is reported.

Reproducibility resources.value: Source dataset/codebook citation and core algorithms/ranges are reported; no code repository, prompts package, exact open-code model, full hyperparameter/search state, or seeds are reported.

Author-reported limitations.value: One dataset, one datatype, and one named theme-generation LLM; performance may vary by domain/dataset/model; t-SNE can distort global structure; human supervision is needed for contextual refinement.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concerns: the open-code generator is unidentified; exact analyzed transcript subset and outlier/coverage rate are unclear; hyperparameters are optimized and evaluated on the same corpus; four flat generated labels are compared with a deep hierarchical human codebook through unspecified alignment; embedding similarity is not independent interpretive validation; no human evaluator reviews source grounding, completeness, or theme usefulness.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Direct comparator for cluster-based inductive pipelines and their validation failure modes. It strengthens the case for held-out evaluation, source traceability, stability/coverage reporting, and human interpretive review beyond embedding similarity.
